column12: launched at 1435 with the Ryujo as its objective ... originally 30 dive bombers and 8 torpedo planes; Ryujo, a heavy cruiser and three destroyers 'bearing 317 T., distance 198 miles from our force' (Enterprise scouts, 1440)

Saratoga was about 5-8 mi from Enterprise (ONI says carriers about 5 miles apart; Cv6 report says Saratoga 10-15 mi on disengaged side later). Ryujo was steering SW at ~30 kn toward the US force (closing). Strike found Ryujo only at 1606 at 06-30S 160-45E (after chasing a second sighting 75 mi NE of Ryujo), attack began 1620, i.e. about 91 min to find it. One SBD and one TBF turned back mechanical. Groups recovered Saratoga ~1845 and after sunset; 'Not a pilot, crewman, or plane of the Saratoga attack group was lost'. Return carrier position not stated. No fuel loss.

Idea of striking Ryujo earlier was abandoned for fear planes 'would not be able to return before nightfall' (doctrine.md). 7 F4F stayed as CAP. Planes flew on 'following instructions' to Henderson Field (all but one TBF) and spent the night there: 36 landed ashore. Why ashore: ONI says only 'following instructions'; inferred reason: the convoy was a search target far from the carrier and recovery on return was not expected (not stated). Next morning the group, minus two SBD forced back to the island field, rejoined Saratoga about 1130 (deferred rendezvous 0800 -> 1100).

Report uses 'zone plus 10' clock and writes the launch time as '090'; ONI shows 0700 (different zone, not converted). OUTCOMES: no Hornet fighter returned to the ship: they stayed with the SBD until forced to head for Midway for lack of gas; 5 pilots rescued (ONI: 8). 13 SBD of Bombing 8 landed at Midway for lack of gas, 2 in the lagoon out of gas; 11 gassed and returned to Hornet 1727. Scouting 8 and Bombing 8 never found the enemy. 15 TBDs (Waldron) found it and were lost to combat.

column19: Held: 17 scout bombers (half the bomber squadron), reason: two further carriers were hoped to be found; the 17 sent against the two reported.

column6: as reported before launch: "1 CV, 2 BB, 3 CA, 4 DD" (Yorktown scout, 1645)

column19: Sent: 24 VSB (11 with a 1000-lb bomb, 13 with a 500-lb), no torpedo planes, no fighters. Zone plus 10. No reason for the size is stated; the morning torpedo squadron had been largely lost.

column6: as supposed before launch: two or three burning carriers, 1 or 2 battleships, cruisers and destroyers, bearing 278, 162 miles
column12: At 1803 commenced launching the second attack group, consisting of 16 VSBs. The target was then assumed to bear 278° T., distant 162 miles and was supposed to consists of two or three burning CVs, 1 or 2 BBs, CAs and DDs.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ships/logs/CV/cv8-Midway.html (para. 10)
column19: Sent: 16 VSB. No torpedo planes or fighters. Enterprise sent 24 VSB the same evening (row above).

column6: as reported before launch: "1 burning CV, 2 BB, 3 CA, 4 DD" at 1000 (about 230 miles)

column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ships/logs/CV/cv6-Midway (Action, 5 June, 1700)
column19: Sent: 32 VSB with a 500-lb bomb each, no fighters, no torpedo planes. The objective was not found; a cruiser or destroyer was attacked. Zone plus 10.

column6: as thought before launch: 2 BB, 4 CA, 1 CV and some DD, 240 miles from Midway
column12: At 1712, commenced launching the attack group, consisting of 26 VSBs. The enemy force at this time was thought to bear 325° T., distant 240 miles from Midway, and to consist of 2 BBs, 4 CAs, 1 CV and some DDs.

column19: Sent: 26 VSB only. No major enemy force was found.

column6: as reported before launch: 2 CA and 2 DD (about 0930 contact report)
column12: Commenced launching attack group composed of 31 VSB, 3 VT, 12 VF, position of objective given as of 1350

column12: Lieut. Tomonaga, Organization #5 composed of 36 ship-based fighters, 36 ship-based bombers, and 36 ship-based torpedo planes, took off to attack Midway.

Held: the fleet had "Organization Number 4 (ship-based torpedo planes) stand by in readiness to act against any enemy surface vessels" (next row). A base target, not a ship target.

column6: aircraft held ready against enemy ships; the aircraft listed as ready by carrier
column12: Prior to this and subsequent to the take off of the initial attack unit, the fleet had Organization Number 4 (ship-based torpedo planes) stand by in readiness to act against any enemy surface vessels. ... (Akagi: 3 ship-based fighters; 18 ship-based attack planes. Kaga: 3 ship-based fighters; 27 ship-based attack planes. Hiryu: 3 ship-based fighters; 18 ship-based bom­bers. Soryu: 3 ship-based fighters; 18 ship-based bombers).
column14: https://midway1942.com/docs/usn_pub_02.shtml (section 1)
column19: Held back from the Midway strike: 12 fighters and 81 attack planes (18 + 27 + 18 + 18) in four carriers, listed as the force to go against the enemy ships. The torpedoes had been exchanged for land bombs by an order of 0415, and the force was not launched: "we would await the return of the Midway attack unit". Tokyo time.

column6: as reported before launch: "1 carrier, 5 cruisers, and 5 destroyers" at 0500, bearing 10 degrees, 240 miles from Midway
column12: At 0500, the enemy composed of 1 carrier, 5 cruisers, and 5 destroyers, was sighted in position bearing 10 degrees, distance 240 miles from Midway. ... At 0758, Hiryu's attack unit (6 fighters and 18 bombers) took off and carried out the attack.
column14: https://midway1942.com/docs/usn_pub_02.shtml (section 1)
column19: Sent: 6 fighters and 18 bombers = 24, at 0758 Tokyo time, by the carrier division commander, after the other three carriers were damaged. A later page (not read) lists the planes; this account gives the size only.

column5: hiryu attack unit (second, with fighters of kaga and a torpedo plane of akagi)

With this information at hand, the Hiryu attack unit (4 fighters and 9 torpedo planes, supplemented by 2 fighters from the Kaga and 1 torpedo plane from the Akagi) was ordered to the attack.

column19: Sent: 4 + 2 fighters and 9 + 1 torpedo planes = 16. At 1240 (Tokyo time) Hiryu "only had 6 fighters, 5 bombers, and 4 torpedo planes left" after the three attacks (same section).

column6: as reported: one carrier, two heavy cruisers and one destroyer (0935 report, received 1017); Ryujo the objective
column12: The Saratoga attack group, which had been held in readiness pending the outcome of the second Enterprise search flight, was launched at 1435 with the Ryujo as its objective. The group originally consisted of 30 dive bombers and 8 torpedo planes and was led by Comdr. Felt, the Air Group Commander.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-ESols/USN-CN-ESolomons-4.html (printed p. 56)
column19: Sent: 30 dive bombers and 8 torpedo planes = 38; no fighter escort is named in the passage. One bomber and one torpedo plane returned with mechanical trouble. The report of 0935 was one carrier, two heavy cruisers and one destroyer (printed p. 54, also row 2186). Reason for the hold: more definite word (p. 54).

column6: Ryujo and a cruiser, as found
column12: As Comdr. Felt approached, he ordered seven dive bombers and two torpedo planes to attack the cruiser and the remaining planes to concentrate on the carrier.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-ESols/USN-CN-ESolomons-4.html (printed p. 57)
column19: A division of the group on arrival, after launch: 7 dive bombers and 2 torpedo planes against the cruiser, the rest (21 + 5) against the carrier. As the carrier avoided hits, Felt ordered the first nine to join the assault on the carrier. Not a division made before launch.

column6: enemy ships at 06-10S 162-50E; launched to clear the deck on word of an enemy air attack
column12: At the same time as the Enterprise planes were sent off, the Saratoga launched her remaining SBD's and TBF's, two planes of VB-3 and five of VT-8.

column19: Sent: 2 SBD and 5 TBF = 7, with no escort. The reason is "word was received of the impending enemy air attack, and the planes were ordered to clear the ship". They proceeded to a position given by Enterprise and found 4 heavy cruisers, 6 light cruisers and 6 to 8 destroyers at 1805. Compare the Enterprise group of 11 SBD, 7 TBF and 7 F4F (rows 2190, 239).

column6: four Japanese ships, probably destroyers, bombarding Guadalcanal
column12: About midnight on the 24th four Japanese ships, probably destroyers, began bombarding our positions on Guadalcanal. ... Between 0245 and 0300 eight dive bombers were sent out from Henderson Field.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-ESols/USN-CN-ESolomons-5.html (printed p. 70)
column19: Sent: 8 dive bombers, against four reported ships. Three located four destroyers and hit one. No escort or reserve stated.

column6: enemy carriers sought (no target reported); an occupation force found at 0835
column12: Just before dawn eight dive bombers with fighter escort left Henderson Field to search for enemy carriers.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-ESols/USN-CN-ESolomons-6.html (printed p. 71)
column19: Sent: 8 dive bombers with a fighter escort of a number not given. They found one large and three small transports with a heavy cruiser, light cruisers and four destroyers and hit the large (14,000-ton) transport and the heavy cruiser. A strike sent without a reported target.

column6: as reported: carriers of Task Force 61 (Chikuma plane, shot down before it gave a position)
column12: 1250 Upon receiving a CHIKUMA search plane sighting report of TF-61's carriers (SARATOGA and ENTERPRISE; TF-18's WASP had been detached south to refuel at 1623 23 August) CarDiv 1 launches a strike. ... SHOKAKU puts up 18 dive-bombers and four fighters led by LtCdr. Seki Mamoru. ZUIKAKU launched nine dive-bombers led by Lt. Otsuka Reijiro and six fighters at 1300 to join them.

column12: 1400 CarDiv 1 launches a second strike. SHOKAKU sends 9 dive-bombers and 3 fighters, joining 18 dive-bombers and 6 fighters from ZUIKAKU.
column14: https://www.combinedfleet.com/Zuikak.htm (Zuikaku tabular record, entry for 24 August 1942)
column19: Sent: 27 dive bombers and 9 fighters = 36. Led by Lt. Takahashi Sadamu; it did not find the American carriers.

column6: torpedo planes held in reserve on 24 August
column12: Torpedo armed planes are to be held in reserve till follow-up strikes.
column14: https://www.combinedfleet.com/Zuikak.htm (Zuikaku tabular record, entry for 24 August 1942, 0415)
column19: The held aircraft: torpedo-armed planes kept for follow-up strikes, with the dive-bomber strike made ready first. No number is given.

column6: as reported before launch: 2 enemy CV at 08-51S 164-30E (1250 despatch from Curtiss), 360 miles
column12: At 1250 October 25, 1942 (Zone minus 12) a despatch was received from CURTISS reporting 2 enemy CV's in latitude 08°-51'S., longitude 164°-30' E., course 145° T., speed 25. ... and at 1520 launched 11 VF, 12 VSB, and 6 VTB with the Group Commander as an attack group to follow up the search.
column14: https://web.archive.org/web/2023/http://www.cv6.org/ship/logs/action19421026.htm (Events of 16-25 October)
column19: Sent: 11 VF, 12 VSB, 6 VTB = 29 and the group commander. The group did not make contact and lost seven aircraft on return in the dark. The report was 360 miles off. A CO's comment later in the report calls the sending of this group a decision the OTC took with information of carriers "at course and speed given, made contact practicable".

column6: as reported before launch: 2 CV at 200 miles bearing 300 (report received 0750)
column12: The BB contact report was received at 0730 and the CV contact report at 0750. ... At 0847 ENTERPRISE attack group of 8 VF, 8 VTB (armed with torpedoes), 3 VSB (armed with 1000-lb bombs) and 1 VTB (the Group Commander) were launched.
column14: https://web.archive.org/web/2023/http://www.cv6.org/ship/logs/action19421026.htm (Action of 26 October)
column19: Sent: 8 VF, 9 VTB (8 + the commander), 3 VSB = 20. The contact: "2 CV at 200 miles on bearing 300" and, in another sector, "2 BB, 1 CA, 7 DD at 170 miles on bearing 275". Compare the Hornet waves (rows below); the ONI count is the same but names the commander separately.

column6: Enterprise attack group of 26 October (the captain's comment)
column12: This group comprised all flyable planes on board and consisted of 20 planes, 8 of which were fighters and one the CEAG. Obviously it was far from an ideal attack group; however, the need for getting them off promptly in order to prevent their being caught on deck by an imminent air attack, and also to get them out to the attack before the enemy carriers opened out too far, were undoubtedly factors in the O.T.C.'s decision.
column14: https://web.archive.org/web/2023/http://www.cv6.org/ship/logs/action19421026.htm (comments of the Commanding Officer)
column19: An after-action judgement and the stated reasons for the size: all flyable aircraft sent; haste to avoid being caught on deck, and to reach the carriers before they opened out. The passage says "far from an ideal attack group"; it does not say the number was too small for the target.

column6: carrier strikes against reliably reported carriers
column12: At such crucial times, we sacrifice much of the power of an attack group for these searches and for inner air and intermediate air patrols. ... It is suggested that, when enemy carriers are reliably reported where we can hit them, we deliver a full strength attack upon them rather than reducing our striking force to search for possible additional carriers or other forces which if found could not be attacked.
column14: https://web.archive.org/web/2023/http://www.cv6.org/ship/logs/action19421026.htm (comments of the Commanding Officer)
column19: A judgement on search against strike strength, not a number for a named target.

column6: as reported before launch: Shokaku and what was thought to be Zuikaku, 210 miles northwest of Task Force KING (first wave)
column12: Upon receipt of the search planes' report of contact with enemy carriers, Admiral Kinkaid ordered an attack group launched to strike the Shokaku and what was thought to be the Zuikaku, now steaming about 210 miles to the northwest of Task Force KING. Beginning at 0830, the Hornet launched two waves of planes. The first consisted of 15 SBD-3's of Bombing Squadron EIGHT and Scouting Squadron EIGHT, 6 TBF-1's of Torpedo Squadron SIX, and 8 F4F-4's of Fighting Squadron 72.
column14: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D207-PURL-gpo172665/pdf/GOVPUB-D207-PURL-gpo172665.pdf (printed p. 37)
column19: Sent: 15 SBD, 6 TBF, 8 F4F = 29. Two carriers reported; the Hornet's two waves together sent 54 (next row). The Santa Cruz narrative gives the waves flying separately "to save time and fuel".

column12: The second Hornet wave, which began taking off at 0915, was made up of 9 SBD-3's and 9 TBF-1's, with 7 F4F-4's as escorts.
column14: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D207-PURL-gpo172665/pdf/GOVPUB-D207-PURL-gpo172665.pdf (printed p. 37)
column19: Sent: 9 SBD, 9 TBF, 7 F4F = 25. With the first wave 54 aircraft of the Hornet, and 20 of the Enterprise, against two reported carriers.

column12: In the meantime, at 0900, the Enterprise began launching 3 SBD-3's of Bombing Squadron TEN, 8 TBF-1's of Torpedo Squadron TEN, and 8 F4F-4's of Fighting Squadron TEN. Lt. Comdr. Richard K. Gaines, the Enterprise Air Group Commander, also took off with this flight in a TBF.
column14: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D207-PURL-gpo172665/pdf/GOVPUB-D207-PURL-gpo172665.pdf (printed p. 37)
column19: Sent: 3 SBD, 8 TBF, 8 F4F and the commander's TBF = 20. The Enterprise's own report gives 0847 and the same numbers (row above).

column6: as reported: one Saratoga-class carrier and 15 other ships, 210 miles (0458)
column12: 0458 Nagumo receives sighting report from a SHOKAKU search plane of one Saratoga-class CV and 15 other ships bearing 125 degrees, distance 210 miles from Kido Butai. He orders immediate launch of the spotted strike ... 0510 SHOKAKU launches 4 fighters and 20 torpedo planes. At 0525 ZUIKAKU launches 21 dive-bombers led by Lt. Takahashi Sadamu with 8 fighters
column14: https://www.combinedfleet.com/Zuikak.htm (Zuikaku tabular record, entry for 26 October 1942)
column19: Sent: 4 + 8 fighters, 20 torpedo planes, 21 dive bombers = 53, a strike already "spotted" on the flight decks. The site's clock.

column12: 0610 SHOKAKU launches 3 CAP and her second strike wave of 5 fighters and 20 dive-bombers under command of Lt. Seki Mamoru.
column14: https://www.combinedfleet.com/Zuikak.htm (Zuikaku tabular record, entry for 26 October 1942)
column19: Sent: 5 fighters and 20 dive bombers from Shokaku. The entry adds that Zuikaku's share (4 fighters and 16 torpedo planes) left about 0700. The site says Nagumo "decided to split the strike, bearing the lessons of Midway in mind."

column5: vt-10 and marine air group (henderson field)
column6: as reported before launch: 26 ships, including 6 seaplane tenders, 126 miles bearing 310
column12: 7 torpedo planes of VT-10, now operating from Guadalcanal, 18 Marine scout bombers, and 12 Marine fighters took off on a contact report of 26 ships, including 6 seaplane tenders, 126 miles away on a bearing of 310° T.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-Guadalcanal/USN-CN-Guadalcanal-2.html (printed p. 53)

column6: the transports of the convoy (about 12 transports and 6 to 8 light cruisers reported on arrival)
column12: At 1255 seventeen scout bombers, including 2 VB-10 and fifteen Marine planes, 8 Marine torpedo bombers, and 8 fighters, left Guadalcanal to attack the transports.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-Guadalcanal/USN-CN-Guadalcanal-2.html (printed pp. 53 to 54)

column6: six cruisers and four destroyers found; heavy and light cruisers
column12: At 1115 the attack group found an enemy force "of about six cruisers and four destroyers" 25 miles to the northwest. After searching for the possible carrier reported by Lt. Gibson, Lt. Comdr. James R. Lee, commanding VS-10 and the attack group, directed the five VB-10 pilots to bomb the heavy cruisers. ... Meanwhile the 11 VS-10 pilots had attacked the light cruisers.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/USN-CN-Guadalcanal/USN-CN-Guadalcanal-2.html (printed p. 51)
column19: A division on arrival, after launch: 5 VB-10 aircraft against the heavy cruisers, 11 VS-10 against the light cruisers, after a search for a carrier reported by Lt. Gibson. Not a division made before launch.

column14: https://web.archive.org/web/20251208162046/https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room/title-list-alphabetically/w/war-damage-reports/uss-north-carolina-bb55-war-damage-report-no-61.html (section III, III-2)

column12: At about 1450-30, while NORTH CAROLINA was starting to swing right from course 280° true in conformity with HORNET which had been observed to start turning right, MUSTIN (TF17) reported by TBS: "Torpedo passed astern headed for you." When this report was received by NORTH CAROLINA, MUSTIN bore about 60° on the port bow, distant about 1200 yards, apparently regaining screening station for the base course.

column6: torpedo wake, missed astern by 4-5 ft
column12: About 1454, while accelerating and swinging right, a torpedo wake was sighted two points forward of the port beam distant 1000 yards. This torpedo barely missed astern (about 4 to 5 feet) because of the accelerating speed and swing to the right.

column6: Task Force 14 (Saratoga, a heavy cruiser, two destroyers)
column12: At 1841, while patrolling 270 miles NE of Johnston Island, I-6 sights a destroyer and crash-dives. column6: Yorktown with a screen of six destroyers (one mile away) and Vireo towing
column12: At 0410, one of I-168's lookouts spots YORKTOWN about 12 miles away. At 0600, Tanabe spots the first destroyers. He submerges and slows to three knots. As he closes, he sees six destroyers circling a mile away. The minesweeper VIREO has YORKTOWN in tow.

column12: 0755 Saw masts over horizon. While making this observation we were strafed by aircraft. Changed depth to 100 feel Echo-ranging first heard at this time.

column6: formation: one battleship (ISE class per Nautilus) and three cruisers

Decided to attack the battleship and changed course to draw ahead. Sighted and bombed by plane. A cruiser of the JINTSU class approached to attack with depth charges. At least two ships were echo-ranging on the NAUTILUS.

column5: JINTSU class cruiser (Nautilus identification; Nagara per Bates and combinedfleet)
column12: 0810 JINTSU class cruiser dropped pattern of S depth charges followed seven minutes later by pattern of 6 depth charges.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 42)
column19: First pattern is printed "S depth charges" in the text layer (probably 5); second pattern 6, seven minutes later.

column12: 0819 Went to 90 feet to avoid scouting planes. Nine depth charges dropped at distance of about 1,000 yards. When attack ceased, planed up to periscope depth to observe.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 44)
column19: Range given as about 1,000 yards, converted x0.9144. Nautilus had gone to 90 feet to avoid scouting planes.

column19: Estimate on the Torpedo Data Computer: range 4,500 yards (x0.9144), angle on the bow 80 degrees starboard, speed 25 knots. Nautilus says ships were moving across the field at high speed and circling away, the battleship firing a starboard broadside at the periscope; #9 deck torpedo ran hot in the tube from a sheared retaining pin.

column6: battleship (ISE class per Nautilus; Kirishima per combinedfleet)
column12: 0825 Fired #1 tube at battleship followed by #2 tube with a 1° right offset. After firing #2 it was found that #1 had not fired. Battleship changed course to the left and headed directly away. Range to battle ship had now increased to 5,000 yards and track was 1800. Held further fire. During this time echo ranging by surface ships was continuous and accurate. Immediately after our firing at the battleship, the JINTSU type cruiser headed for NAUTILUS.

column19: Two tubes ordered, one torpedo left (tube #1 failed to fire). Range 4,500 yds est. at 0824. The target turned away; range opened to 5,000 yards. Bates and combinedfleet say the torpedo missed.

column12: 0830 Went to 150 feet. Depth charge attack began. 0846 Ordered periscope depth. Battleship and other accompanying ships, except JINTSU type cruiser, were well out of range. Echo-ranging by cruiser was still accurate.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 50)
column19: Depth charge attack began after Nautilus went to 150 feet; at 0846 the cruiser was still echo-ranging accurately.

column12: 0900 Raised periscope and sighted aircraft carrier bearing 013° relative. Carrier was distant 16,000 yards and was changing course continuously. She did not appear to be damaged, but was overhung by anti-aircraft bursts. NAUTILUS was on a converging course. While making this observation the JINTSU type cruiser began to close again at high speed.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 52)
column19: Range 16,000 yards converted x0.9144. Carrier was changing course continuously, overhung by anti-aircraft bursts; the JINTSU type cruiser began to close again at high speed.

column6: JINTSU class cruiser (as reported; destroyer Arashi per Bates and Nagumo report)
column12: 0910 When cruiser reached 2,500 yards fired #2 torpedo tube. Cruiser was observed to change course.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 54)
column19: Fired #2 tube when cruiser reached 2,500 yards (x0.9144); cruiser seen to change course. Second source for the shot on file as event 8044 (Bates) and 8018 (Nagumo report).

column12: 0918 A cruiser attacked with 6 depth charges. These were more accurately placed than previous charges. Went to 200 feet, used evasive tactics at slow speed, but continued advance to close the carrier. Cruiser continued echoranging and at 0933 two of her depth charges landed close.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 56)
column19: Charges more accurately placed than earlier ones; at 0933 two more landed close. Nautilus went to 200 feet at slow speed.

column12: 0955 Echo-ranging ceased. Ordered periscope depth to estimate the situation. On looking found that the entire formation first seen, including the attacking cruisers had departed. The carrier previously seen was no longer in sight.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 58)
column19: Entire formation including the attacking cruisers had departed. Nautilus then closed smoke to the north.

column6: burning aircraft carrier (reported as SORYU class)
column12: 1145 Identified the source of smoke as a burning carrier. The carrier was still about 8 miles away and was in latitude 30°-13′ N., Longitude 179°-17′ W. Decided to overtake if possible and to attack.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 62)
column19: Carrier about 8 miles away. Identity: Nautilus reported Soryu; the question whether the ship was Kaga is raised by other sources.

column6: burning carrier with two cruisers about two miles ahead
column12: 1253 Range decreased. Sighted two cruisers escorting the carrier. Tentatively identified CV as a carrier of the SORYU class. The carrier was on even keel and the hull appeared to be undamaged. There were no flames and the fire seemed to be under control. Accompanying cruisers were about two miles ahead of the carrier.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 66)
column19: Nautilus saw the carrier on an even keel, hull apparently undamaged, no flames, fire seeming under control.

column12: 1300 The CV, which bad been making 2-3 knots when the approach began, was now stopped. At closer range it was seen that efforts were being made by boats under her bow to pass a towing hawser and many men were seen working on the forecastle. The decision had to be made in which order to attack the targets presented. Attack on the cruisers and later on the carrier was considered, but the remaining capacity of the battery would not allow a further chase of several miles to catch the moving cruisers, even if it were possible to overtake them. The decision was therefore made to complete the destruction of the CV before she could be repaired or taken in tow. Approach continued at periscope depth. An approach course was chosen to give torpedo hits on the starboard or island side of the carrier. During the next hour a repeated check was made of the silhouettes of American and Japanese carriers in order to be certain of the identity of the target. The target was a carrier of the SORYU class.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 68)
column19: Carrier had been making 2-3 knots, now stopped; boats under her bow trying to pass a towing hawser; many men on the forecastle. Nautilus chose to attack the carrier rather than the cruisers because of battery capacity.

column12: 1359 Fired three torpedoes at the carrier from periscope depth. Attempts to fire the 4th torpedo were unsuccessful. Immediately prior to firing each torpedo, the Torpedo Data Computer generated bearing was checked by a periscope bearing. Mean run of torpedoes was 2, 700 yards.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 70)
column19: Range = mean run 2,700 yards x0.9144. Attempts to fire a fourth torpedo were unsuccessful. Second source for event 8045/8046/8047.

column12: The wakes of the torpedoes were observed through the periscope until the torpedoes struck the target. Red flames appeared along the length of the ship from the bow to amidships.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 70)
column19: This is Nautilus's claim (all 5 officers in the conning tower saw it). The editor's note in the same text says Japanese survivors testified two of three missed and one hit was a dud.

column12: 1405 Fired last of three torpedoes at the carrier. Cruisers began reversing course at high speed and started to echorange.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 72)
column19: Last of three torpedoes; cruisers began reversing course at high speed and echo-ranging.

column12: 1410 Cruiser passed directly over the top of the NAUTILUS. Changed course to 190’7 and went to 300 feet. A prolonged depth charge attack now began.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 74)
column19: Nautilus went to 300 feet; a prolonged depth charge attack followed. At 1610 she came to periscope depth and escorts were no longer in sight.

column12: 1840 Heard heavy subsurface explosions and went to depth charge stations. A search by periscope failed to reveal any object in the vicinity except the still greater cloud of black smoke from burning oil. If the carrier was not found by patrol planes which searched the vicinity the following morning, the Commanding Officer believes that she was destroyed at this time by fire and internal explosions. He did not however actually see her sink.
column14: https://archive.navalsubleague.org/?p=1765, "USS NAUTILUS - First War Patrol", NARRATIVE (all times local) June 4, 1942 (text line 78)
column19: Heavy subsurface explosions heard; the commanding officer did not see the carrier sink.

column12: Two of the cruisers attempted to close for a kill and nine depth charges were dropped at a distance of about 1000 yards.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ships/dafs/SS/ss168.html (DANFS USS Nautilus II (SS-168), 4 June paragraphs) (text line 18)

column6: TG 7.1: Flying Fish and Cachalot on arc 310-350, 50 miles; Cuttlefish 700 miles due west (station patrol)
column12: two submarines, the FLYING FISH and the CACHALOT were disposed on the arc 310-350° (T), distant 50 miles from Midway. column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/rep/Rainbow5-USN.html (HyperWar transcription of WPPac-46 from the Pearl Harbor hearings; line 3656 of saved text rainbow5-usn.txt)
column19: Says: Submarines serving as fleet forces from outlying bases are under a fleet task force commander, with missions set by broader strategy rather than local defence. Two classes of boat: base local defence under the base commander, fleet forces under the task force commander. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column5: US Pacific Fleet planners (Rainbow Five estimate of enemy action)
column12: Submarine raids and observation off Oahu and outlying islands and along our lines of communication.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/rep/Rainbow5-USN.html (HyperWar transcription of WPPac-46 from the Pearl Harbor hearings, printed p. 42 (no PDF page markers in text); line 1655 of saved text rainbow5-usn.txt)
column19: Says: The US plan expects Japanese submarines to raid and observe off Oahu and the outlying islands and along US lines of communication. This is the planners' view of what the enemy would do in the area subject to US patrol plane search; it fits what the 1942 record shows later. Heading 5, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column5: US Pacific Fleet planners (Rainbow Five estimate of initial Japanese deployment)
column12: Raiding and observation forces widely distributed in the Pacific, and submarines in the Hawaiian Area.
column14: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/rep/Rainbow5-USN.html (HyperWar transcription of WPPac-46 from the Pearl Harbor hearings, printed p. 22 (no PDF page markers in text); line 1157 of saved text rainbow5-usn.txt)
column19: Says: The estimated initial Japanese deployment includes submarines in the Hawaiian Area and, in the Mandates, a strong concentration of submarines and light patrol craft. Second item is "Strong concentration of submarines and light surface patrol craft in the Mandates" (R5 line 1152); the estimate comes from the plan's paragraph 1334. Heading 5, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column5: Commander Submarine Force Pacific Fleet, USF 25(A)
column12: The primary task of the submarine is to inflict maximum damage on enemy ships and shipping. This task shall be carried out at every opportunity unless expressly forbidden.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 1 (no PDF page markers in text); line 58 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: The primary task is to sink or damage enemy ships and shipping at every opportunity unless forbidden. Date is the publication date of the edition (February 1944); doctrine is described as drawn from experience and from the War Instructions. Heading 1, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: During probable long periods before fleet action occurs, submarines may be usefully employed in the following tasks: Patrol. (Including commerce destruction). Scouting. Screening. Mining. Reconnaissance. Services to aircraft.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 1 (no PDF page markers in text); line 39 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: Tasks named are patrol (with commerce destruction), scouting, screening, mining, reconnaissance, services to aircraft, escort in exceptional cases and delivering mail or personnel. Figure as read: 7 tasks listed (8 with mail and personnel). The quote stops after the sixth item; escort and mail follow. The list is in no stated priority order but the next paragraph names attack as the primary task. Heading 1, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: When submarine attacks can be coordinated
column12: Such attacks by two or more submarines may be coordinated when movements of the enemy are predictable or are restricted to narrow limits by other factors. These conditions are usually satisfied when it is evident that the enemy is approaching a specific objective.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 3 (no PDF page markers in text); line 146 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: Coordinated attack by several boats is feasible when the enemy's movements are predictable, usually when he is making for a specific objective such as a base to be established or attacked. The text goes on to list stationary and moving objectives. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Geometry of a submarine line across enemy approach
column12: They resolve themselves into individual attacks by two or more submarines, when the submarine line covers a wide front normal to the enemy advance in order to provide for contingencies of freedom of enemy movement.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 3 (no PDF page markers in text); line 153 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: A line spread wide across the enemy's advance covers uncertainty in his track but gives separate individual attacks and few chances for attack. The same paragraph says a line normal to the advance "has the disadvantage of offering comparatively few opportunities for attack". No spacing in miles is given in this chapter. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Geometry of a submarine line along enemy approach
column12: If the enemy approach is positively known to be confined to narrow limits, the submarine line can then be parallel to the direction of advance, and the coordinated attack becomes a series of individual attacks.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 3 (no PDF page markers in text); line 156 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: If the enemy approach is certain to stay within narrow limits, boats can be placed in a line parallel to his advance, and each makes an attack in turn. The text warns that this risks no attack at all if the estimate of the enemy track is wrong. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Submarines and other forces: who coordinates
column12: Submarine operations can be coordinated with, but not closely combined with, those of surface ships or aircraft. If such coordination is desired, slow submerged speed and lack of reliability in communications while submerged, place the burden of coordination on the other units involved
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 3 (no PDF page markers in text); line 172 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: Submarines are coordinated with, not closely combined with, other forces, and because of slow speed and poor communications submerged the other forces must carry the burden of coordination. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Position of a boat after missing the enemy fleet
column12: If used in connection with fleet battle, a submarine losing contact, or a unit which definitely knows that the enemy fleet has gone by without presenting favorable opportunity for attack, may be expected to trail or to take position on the enemy's retirement line or between him and his most probable base.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 3 (no PDF page markers in text); line 185 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: A boat that has lost contact or let the enemy fleet pass is expected to trail it or take station on its line of retirement or between it and its most probable base. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: How orders reach a submerged boat
column12: When submarines are patrolling submerged during daylight, information and directives will be disseminated by "F" method on regular schedules, circumstances permitting. All such communications will be retransmitted at night after all units have surfaced in order to insure delivery.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 9 (no PDF page markers in text); line 542 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: Orders and information go to submerged patrolling boats on regular schedules by a low-frequency "F" method, and are sent again at night when all boats have surfaced to be sure of delivery. In the same section the file gives low-frequency reception of 2,000 to 3,000 miles from a high-power shore station with the loop 15 to 20 feet down. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Own submarines used against enemy submarines
column12: the enemy submarine will have to remain submerged throughout daylight hours or risk the possibility of submarine attacks. This has the effect of forcing him to do all battery charging at night or in thick weather
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-1.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 1, printed p. 10 (no PDF page markers in text); line 558 of saved text ssdoct-1.txt)
column19: Says: If own boats may be near, an enemy submarine has to stay down by day and charge batteries at night, which slows it and wears on its crew. The text adds that the mere presence of own boats ahead of the fleet reduces enemy submarines' effectiveness in holding a striking position ahead of their fleet. Heading 6, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: That all commanding officers appreciate the importance of information of the enemy and exchange of information relative to own operations, and that the making of contact reports, whenever possible, will be automatic.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 25 (no PDF page markers in text); line 17 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Doctrine assumes boats' contact reports will be made automatically whenever possible. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: Important information and directives will be passed to submarines on prearranged radio schedules.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 25 (no PDF page markers in text); line 49 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Orders and information reach boats on prearranged radio schedules. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Why no positions are prescribed for submarines in a fleet disposition
column12: The accepted doctrine that submarine operations may be coordinated with, but not closely combined with those of surface craft, is the primary reason why no positions are prescribed for submarines in fleet approach, contact, and battle disposition.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 26 (no PDF page markers in text); line 57 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: No fixed positions are prescribed for boats in a fleet disposition because their operations are coordinated with, not combined with, those of surface ships. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Position of a submarine unit in fleet approach
column12: During fleet approach formations, the submarine unit will usually be disposed well in the van of own main body, probably in a scouting line formation dependent upon information of the enemy fleet.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 26 (no PDF page markers in text); line 83 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: During a fleet approach the submarine unit is usually well ahead of the main body, probably in a scouting line shaped by what is known of the enemy. No distance in miles is given in this passage. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Position of boats once battle starts
column12: If the submarine attack has not been executed before the battle starts, submarines should seek ... positions ahead of the enemy battle line or in areas through which the enemy may be expected to pass.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 26 (no PDF page markers in text); line 112 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Boats that have not attacked before the battle begins should get ahead of the enemy battle line or into areas the enemy is expected to pass. Quote joins two exact pieces across a page break marker. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: Patrol operations may be ordered to accomplish one or more of the following missions: To attack enemy lines of communication in a particular area or along a particular route or line. To blockade an enemy coastline. To establish control of a sea area. To protect a fleet in an exposed anchorage. To conduct an observation patrol.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 28 (no PDF page markers in text); line 131 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Patrol may be ordered to attack communications in an area or along a route, blockade a coast, establish control of a sea area, protect a fleet in an exposed anchorage, or observe. Figure as read: 5 missions. Heading 1, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Separation of boats from own ships and aircraft
column12: Because of the difficulty of two-way identification, friendly surface vessels and aircraft ordinarily should not be assigned to patrol the same area with submarines.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 28 (no PDF page markers in text); line 148 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Own ships and aircraft are ordinarily not assigned to patrol the same area as own submarines. Relevant to boats operating near Midway, Truk or Kavieng where own aircraft also patrol. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Patrol against shipping near focal points
column12: Submarines operate singly in assigned sectors on the edge of focal and terminal areas and furnish information of enemy shipping to other submarines similarly employed.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 28 (no PDF page markers in text); line 160 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Against shipping, boats work singly in sectors on the edge of focal and terminal areas and pass shipping information to other boats nearby. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: Submarine positions should be shifted frequently to cover variations in shipping routes as well as to evade concentrated anti-submarine effort in areas of operations discovered by the enemy.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 28 (no PDF page markers in text); line 162 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Boat stations should be shifted often to follow changes in shipping routes and to escape anti-submarine effort in areas the enemy has found out. No time interval is given. War Instructions 919 (1944) says the same. Heading 3, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Submarines against an enemy overseas advance
column12: In opposing an overseas advance, submarines may be employed profitably in attrition operations against the enemy force during passage and in attacks at or near its destination.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 28 (no PDF page markers in text); line 168 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Against an overseas advance, boats may profitably wear down the force on passage and attack at or near its destination. The next lines say transports are especially valuable targets. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Where to locate an enemy overseas advance
column12: Search patrol, or observation is required for the first phase. This usually can be done best near the probable destination of the enemy because of the reduced area to be covered. However, the ideal method is to trail the enemy from his point of departure, and, from information supplied by trailing submarines, concentrate attack groups ahead along his assumed course.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 28 (no PDF page markers in text); line 178 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Boats working alone find the enemy best near his probable destination where the area is smaller, but the ideal is to trail him from his point of departure and put attack groups ahead on his assumed course. Direct statement of the placement rule: near the destination, or trailing from departure. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: The scouting distance for submarines on the surface should be not greater than 20 miles and that for submarine submerged should be not greater than 12 miles.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 29 (no PDF page markers in text); line 206 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Scouting distance (spacing) for a boat on the surface is not more than 20 miles and submerged not more than 12 miles. Figure as read: 20 mi surface; 12 mi submerged. "Scouting distance" read as the width one boat covers; the file does not say interval between boats in a line. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Reporting range of a submerged scout
column12: and communication except during darkness is limited to that obtainable with the vertical antenna, which has an effective range of about 100 miles.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 29 (no PDF page markers in text); line 201 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: A scout kept down by day can report by day only through the vertical antenna, range about 100 miles. Figure as read: 100 mi. Context: in waters patrolled by enemy submarines or within range of enemy planes, scouts must stay submerged by day. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: Landing party reconnaissance will be conducted at night by men sent ashore in rubber boats.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-3.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 3, printed p. 32 (no PDF page markers in text); line 307 of saved text ssdoct-3.txt)
column19: Says: Landing-party reconnaissance of a shore is done at night with men in rubber boats from the submarine. The section also lists periscope visual and photographic reconnaissance. Makin raid (August 1942) used this method per Cominch bulletin No. 1. Heading 1, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Response of a boat to a contact report
column12: When the first knowledge of the near presence of the enemy is obtained from a contact report, proceed to attain a position ahead of, and out of sight of, the ship or force (including any screens) reported.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-4.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 4, printed p. 39 (no PDF page markers in text); line 171 of saved text ssdoct-4.txt)
column19: Says: On a contact report a boat is to get ahead of the reported force, out of sight. Heading 3, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Fallback position when a boat cannot get ahead
column12: If unable to reach a position ahead of the enemy, correct procedure is to take up station in an area he is expected to pass through, or to trail so that attack may be made in the event he should reverse course.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/SS-Doct/SS-Doct-4.html (USF 25(A), HyperWar chapter 4, printed p. 39 (no PDF page markers in text); line 174 of saved text ssdoct-4.txt)
column19: Says: A boat that cannot get ahead of the enemy takes station in an area he is expected to pass or trails him. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: What submarines are normally used for
column12: Submarines are normally employed to attack with torpedoes those enemy units whose destruction or damage would most seriously interfere with the successful prosecution of enemy operations.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 44 (no PDF page markers in text); line 88 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: Boats normally torpedo the enemy units whose loss would most upset enemy operations; heavy combatant ships and loaded transports are preferred to light craft. Date is the 1944 edition; the file shows no preface here. The text says the war-instruction chapter refers readers to USF 25 for detail. Heading 1, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Radio silence of a submarine scout
column12: It is also usually necessary for him to observe radio silence except for vital contact reports; otherwise he may be located promptly by radio direction finders, his safety jeopardized, and his usefulness greatly curtailed.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 44 (no PDF page markers in text); line 121 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: A scouting boat usually keeps radio silence except for vital contact reports because radio direction finders can locate it quickly. The text adds transmission at night is possible, accepting the chance of detection. This shows US doctrine named DF as the main risk of reporting. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Reports by boats on patrol in enemy waters
column12: Submarines operating in enemy waters are not required to transmit reports by radio, except on special occasions where the importance of the communication to be transmitted justifies the disclosure of its position
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 45 (no PDF page markers in text); line 151 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: Boats on patrol in enemy waters need not radio reports unless the message is important enough to be worth giving away the position. Contrast with Rainbow Five 1941 task: "Report important enemy movements by radio if success of attack mission is not thereby jeopardized." Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Submarine screen across enemy line of advance
column12: Submarines may be utilized for screening operations and are best employed as a distant screen across an enemy line of advance to inform own forces of any enemy attempting to intercept.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 45 (no PDF page markers in text); line 133 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: The best use of boats as a screen is a distant line across the enemy's line of advance to warn own forces. The next sentence says enemy air activity would seriously reduce the effect. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: Normally this employment requires the stationing of submarines as patrol units near the enemy's known point of departure and along focal points in the ... line of his advance.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 45 (no PDF page markers in text); line 186 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: Against an enemy advance boats are stationed as patrol units near his known point of departure and at focal points along his line of advance. Quote joins two exact pieces over a page marker. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Placement against a fast or choice-of-route enemy
column12: When the enemy's speed is relatively high or when he has the choice of several divergent routes it is best to concentrate our submarines in the vicinity of his known destination, as otherwise he may be able to avoid the areas in which they are disposed.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 46 (no PDF page markers in text); line 191 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: If the enemy is fast or has several routes, boats are concentrated near his known destination, since elsewhere he could avoid them. The text adds this is especially so when only slow submarines are available. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Boats on the enemy's line of retreat
column12: In cases when it is probable that the enemy will retire to a known base or area, such submarines as have been unable to attack during the major engagement and submarines no longer in position to attack but having torpedoes remaining, may be disposed along the enemy's line of retreat for the purpose of attacking as he retires.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 46 (no PDF page markers in text); line 243 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: Boats that did not attack, or are out of position but still have torpedoes, may be placed along the enemy's line of retreat to a known base. Compare Midway, 5-6 June 1942, Cominch bulletin No. 1. Heading 2, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column6: Telling other forces where boats are
column12: Whenever submarines are operating with other forces all ships and aircraft must be informed of the location and probable operations of these submarines.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-9.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 9, printed p. 46 (no PDF page markers in text); line 213 of saved text warinst-9.txt)
column19: Says: All ships and aircraft must be told where operating boats are, including boats ahead of own forces, on scouting lines, in the enemy's probable track and off bases or objectives. Same principle as Rainbow Five 1941. Heading 4, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: When practicable, known submarine waters are avoided. Also effort is made to avoid passing through, or in close proximity to the same waters traversed in the preceding twenty-four hours.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-7.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 7, printed p. 29 (no PDF page markers in text); line 23 of saved text warinst-7.txt)
column19: Says: Known submarine waters are avoided, and a force avoids waters it passed through in the last 24 hours. Figure as read: 24 hours. A 1944 rule; Cominch bulletins of 1942 (Coral Sea, Santa Cruz) criticise carriers staying in one area, so the idea predates it but this wording is the 1944 text. Heading 6, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: Generally speaking, all vessels, even though adequately screened, zigzag in submarine waters.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-7.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 7, printed p. 29 (no PDF page markers in text); line 35 of saved text warinst-7.txt)
column19: Says: Ships zigzag in submarine waters even when screened. Heading 6, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column12: A spacing of one and a half the assured sonar range (determined by bathythermograph) gives a high probability of detection.
column14: https://ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USN/ref/WarInst/WarInst-6.html (War Instructions 1944, HyperWar chapter 6, printed p. 21 (no PDF page markers in text); line 139 of saved text warinst-6.txt)
column19: Says: Screening ships are spaced at one and a half times the assured sonar range for a high chance of detecting a submarine. Figure as read: 1.5 x assured sonar range. Bathythermograph basis implies this is a later-war rule. The screen is set at a distance allowing at least one depth-charge attack before the boat reaches firing range. Heading 6, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column5: Cominch Battle Experience Bulletin No. 1, commentary on Coral Sea (published 1943)
column6: Task forces fuelling at slow speed in one area
column12: A study of the track chart shows that the- Task Forces were seriously exposed to submarine attack during 1-2 May while fueling at slow speed within a restricted area. Enemy has taken advantage ofthis opportunity in later months while our Task Forces operated in same general area at slow speed over a period of several days.
column14: https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA606373/DTIC_ADA606373_djvu.txt (Bulletin No.1, OCR text; line 3142 of saved text DTIC_ADA606373.txt)
column19: Says: Commentary says Task Forces 11 and 17 were exposed to submarine attack while fuelling slowly in a small area on 1-2 May 1942, and that the enemy exploited the same habit in later months when forces stayed several days at low speed in the same area. Date is the event; commentary written later in 1942 or 1943. Relevant to carriers kept in the same waters in August to September 1942. Heading 6, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column5: Yorktown air scout (sighting), Cominch Battle Experience Bulletin No. 1
column6: Japanese submarine near Task Forces 11 and 17 in the Coral Sea
column12: a YORKTOVH air scout sighted an enemy submarine on the surface in Latitude 16° 04' S., Longitude 162° 18' E. , just 32 miles north of Task Force 11 and 17.
column14: https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA606373/DTIC_ADA606373_djvu.txt (Bulletin No.1, OCR text; line 3150 of saved text DTIC_ADA606373.txt)
column19: Says: A Yorktown scout sighted an enemy submarine on the surface 32 miles north of Task Forces 11 and 17 at 1545 on 2 May 1942. Figure as read: 32 mi. OCR "YORKTOVH" kept; coordinates as printed. Heading 5, USN (employment research of 2026-11-23).

column5: Cominch Battle Experience Bulletin No. 1 commentary
column6: US estimate of what the sighted submarine meant
column12: The proximity of the submarine to our surface forces and direction finder radio bearings pointed to the probability of their position having been reported to the enemy.
